Then compare the language. Note words added in brackets, ellipses, reordered clauses, translations, and whether a question was turned into a statement. A viral version may be memorable precisely because an editor shortened it.

## Test attribution, not just chronology

The earliest row wins only the claim “earliest occurrence located.” To say a person actually said or wrote it, connect that person to the source:

  * their voice or appearance in an authentic recording
  * a signed or cataloged document with reliable provenance
  * an official transcript tied to a named event
  * a publication under their name with edition and page information
  * contemporaneous reporting that directly identifies the speaker and setting

Also read what comes before and after. The person may be quoting an opponent, reading a letter, asking a question, or rejecting the very claim later attached to them.

## State the result at the right confidence

Use one of these conclusions:

  * Confirmed primary source: the attributable document or recording contains the words in context.
  * Earliest attributable occurrence located: this is the oldest supported use found, but authorship of the phrase is not proved.
  * Likely source: a strong chain exists with one unresolved link.
  * Misattributed or materially altered: an earlier or primary source shows a different speaker, wording, or context.
  * Unresolved: available evidence does not support a responsible attribution.

Include the exact source location and a short context note, not just a URL. Preserve important web evidence using how to preserve and document a web source. If the source page's date is disputed, continue with how to find the earliest version of a web page.

Gottlob Frege was probably the first philosopher or logician to note that predicating truth or existence does not express anything above and beyond the statement to which it is attributed. He remarked:

    
It is worthy of notice that the sentence "I smell the scent of violets" has the same content as the sentence "it is true that I smell the scent of violets". Nevertheless, the first serious attempt at the formulation of a theory of truth which attempted to systematically define the truth predicate out of existence is attributable to F. P. Ramsey. # When can I omit the subject?

Asked 8 years ago

Modified 8 years ago

Viewed 2k times

[Input]

Can I omit the subject if it has been mentioned in a preceding sentence?

For example, is the phrase inside the parentheses necessary in the below?:

> > The sculpture A exhibits degradation at a seemingly increased rate from 30 years ago. However, the surrounding environment is considered not to have changed at a significant level since (the sculpture was) carved.

  * writing-style
  * writing
  * subjects

Sorted by:

[Input]

In a word: no. You have to have a pronoun or other noun here: “since it was carved”. You can usually omit the subject in the context “Subject predicate and predicate” (e.g., “Sculpture A exhibits degradation and is a cause for concern”), but adjuncts do not permit this kind of subject omission (e.g., you can’t say “Sculpture A exhibits degradation because _ was poorly conserved / since _ was moved / etc.”).

Also, I wouldn’t use the definite article at the start of the first sentence: “Sculpture A exhibits degradation …”.
